edge_031.relationship: Toynbee uses political economy to frame historical questions; North later revises neoclassical assumptions through institutions and change
edge_031.evidence_note: Economic historians use changing theoretical resources: Tawney’s religious-economic questions differ from North’s institutional explanation. Toynbee’s opening lecture explicitly explains this reciprocal use. North’s existing scoped lecture check supports the later distinction; no direct Smith-to-North lineage is claimed. Furtado explicitly invokes Keynes in chapter XXXI while retrospectively interpreting coffee-surplus destruction as support for income and employment. Novais’s1961review welcomes the income-flow analysis but requests structural explanation. No claim that1931policymakers followed Keynes’s1936book is made.

edge_035.relationship: Marsh, Leopold and Sauer supply distinct resources for environmental historical inquiry and teaching
edge_035.evidence_note: Marsh is an environmental precursor; do not derive every environmental-history tradition from Vidal or Annales. Lowenthal documents Marsh’s environmental-history relevance; Cronon recalls workshops modeled on Leopold’s course. These are distinct historical resources, not one direct genealogy. A further named teaching use is Cronon’s Fall 1994 History 901 assignment of Sauer’s 1941 Foreword to Historical Geography. This is separate from the 1925 Morphology essay and establishes a syllabus use, not universal reception. Hewes’s The Suitcase-Farming Frontier (1973) supplies another specific resource: Worster’s 1986 note14 explicitly uses it, and McDean124/note37 identifies Hurt’s use. This shared historical geography does not establish identical causal interpretations. Original Hewes book unread.
edge_035.map_label: Inquiry, landscape training and Sauer reading

edge_123.relationship: questions the nation as a self-contained unit
edge_123.evidence_note: The target is the nation treated as a self-contained explanatory unit, not all histories of political institutions. Connected Histories735–742 and758–762 targets bounded national/area units while retaining difference; Duara’s publisher-described project adds conflicting historical narratives. Neither abolishes political institutions as objects of study.

edge_158.relationship: is reworked in an account of hegemony, intellectuals, and political struggle

edge_201.relationship: Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s demographic reconstructions supply distinct quantitative practices
edge_201.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Henry’s p. 334 and the now-checked Cambridge institutional history replace the earlier generic institutional pointer with specified methods; no universal origin or direct Henry-to-every-Cambridge-technique genealogy is asserted. The French programme is explicitly collaborative: Fleury/Henry1958 credits Goubert and other researchers, and Biraben coauthors the1960 inventory. Henry1978 distinguishes aggregate sampling from the family-reconstitution subset; no isolated-founder attribution is warranted.

edge_215.relationship: shares comparative questions across regions while differing in methods and scale
edge_215.evidence_note: No direct Skocpol → Pomeranz genealogy is asserted. Wong73 quotes Tilly’s definition while distinguishing paths; Subrahmanyam758–759 directly contests Goldstone’s model. The broad comparison remains undirected, alongside a separately recorded specific critique.

edge_348.relationship: Appadurai and Kopytoff offer distinct analyses of circulating value and changing commodity status
edge_348.evidence_note: The primary opening extracts document their conceptual contributions. Douglas and Isherwood supply a further, publisher-supported account of goods as communication. No exclusive disciplinary origin or influence on every historian is claimed. Vickery’s chapter5/note9 explicitly uses Douglas/Isherwood and cites Appadurai’s collection. It does not name Kopytoff in the checked passages, so that individual reception is not inferred. Geary explicitly cites Kopytoff169 and proposes object biographies188 in the same1986 collection. This now supplies a particular historian’s use of the person/commodity problem, with his own limits on evidence189–190.
edge_348.map_label: Circulating value, commodity status and social uses

edge_639.relationship: Subrahmanyam contests Goldstone’s autonomous-state model and ideological partitions
edge_639.evidence_note: Connected Histories758–759 names Revolution and Rebellion1991, objecting to demographic/fiscal sequencing and an eschatological/cyclical partition in light of circulating ideas. Records his criticism; the complete Goldstone book and empirical dispute are not adjudicated. The regional critique was rechecked in the second pass. Goldstone’s separately read preface and France/Spain comparison emphasize institutional conjunctions and divergent outcomes. His self-description therefore differs from the critic’s sharply reductive characterization; these passages are not a reply to Subrahmanyam, and do not settle the disputed ideological categories in the unread chapter 5.

edge_1931.relationship: Uses the Wilson biography attributed to Freud as a negative example of biographical hostility to its subject.

Bullitt, not Freud alone; bibliographic coauthor credit checked against Routledge publisher record, https://www.routledge.com/link/link/p/book/9781138540705 (copyright1966). No complete original or general rejection of psychoanalysis claimed.

edge_1932.relationship: Invokes Lévi-Strauss’s bricolage as an analogy for the singular construction of Menocchio’s culture.
edge_1932.evidence_note: Own2011 paragraph34 describes Ginzburg’s Menocchio through this named conceptual analogy. This establishes the particular use, not direct reading of a specified Lévi-Strauss text or formal mentorship; complete original works unread. Claude Lévi-Strauss is distinct from Giovanni Levi.

edge_1933.relationship: Applies Freudian categories of repression, return and obsession to the changing forms of collective memory.
edge_1933.evidence_note: Own2011 paragraph22 explicitly endorses this conceptual use after discussing Rousso, Joutard and Stora as historical examples. These named mediations remain; no direct reading of a particular Freud text or general equation of individual and collective processes is certified. Coexists with his distinct negative2012 judgment of the Wilson biography.

edge_1934.relationship: Hartog credits Certeau’s reading of Jean de Léry with shaping his questions about Herodotus and otherness, and Certeau’s challenge about unthought historical time with prompting his later temporal inquiry.
edge_1934.evidence_note: Own retrospective Portuguese interview identifies actual reading and intellectual effect,alongside Vidal-Naquet,Vernant,Finley and travel. Hartog recalls the stimulus before1975;editorial note8 identifies the1975collection text,not proof of an earlier book edition. No exclusive genealogy or complete Certeau/Herodotus reading claimed. Own ENS2021 answer separately recalls beginning from Certeau’s challenge that history leaves time unthought and developing regimes of historicity from that provocation. This second retrospective prompt is consolidated in the same influence pair; it establishes no exclusive origin or original Certeau text collation.

edge_1935.relationship: Hartog credits his reading of Lévi-Strauss with an anthropological openness that helped reframe his relation to ancient Greece.
edge_1935.evidence_note: Own2011/2012answer354 explicitly places this reading before and alongside his Indonesian journey and the development of his Herodotus project. It does not identify a particular Lévi-Strauss work or make travel the sole cause;no title/edition is guessed and originals remain unread.

edge_1936.relationship: Hartog identifies Braudel’s writings on history as a resource for his own historiography teaching and reflection.
edge_1936.evidence_note: Own interview355 names La Méditerranée and especially Écrits sur l’histoire,which he read while teaching at Strasbourg after1975. He explicitly never attended Braudel’s seminar and had not originally worked in modern history;the interviewer’s implied early Indonesian Braudel influence is rejected. Original1949/1969works unread.

edge_1937.relationship: Hartog argues that Braudel’s hierarchy of historical durations and treatment of events should themselves be understood in their wartime and postwar setting.
edge_1937.evidence_note: Own interview355 historicizes the program while praising its enlargement of historians’ questions and denying that he means to denounce Braudel or reduce longue durée to refusal of war. This is a qualified challenge to treating the1950s–1960sframework as self-evident;not a claim that wartime context wholly explains it.

edge_1938.relationship: Hartog uses Koselleck’s tension between experience and expectation to formulate the problem of presentism.
edge_1938.evidence_note: Own interview363 explicitly reuses the categories while asking whether their relation has broken down and distinguishing provisional from fuller presentism. The formulation remains a question/heuristic,not a demonstrated universal sequence. Note29 cites a2006edition without a matching complete bibliography entry;original edition/work not guessed and unread.

edge_1939.relationship: Hartog uses Arendt’s image of a gap in time to explore whether presentism represents a pause or a more durable regime.
edge_1939.evidence_note: Own interview363 explicitly borrows the image while retaining uncertainty about its application. Editorial note28 points to a1961reference and Portuguese rendering,but supplies no complete matching bibliographic entry;no original edition or whole Arendt theory is invented. Original text unread.

edge_1940.relationship: Hartog uses Ricœur’s inquiries into narrative,time and historical representation as a resource for reflecting on historians’ own practice.
edge_1940.evidence_note: Own2012answer360 credits Ricœur’s actual reading of historians;369identifies contemporary interpreters as sources for his reflection. Own2011/2013article16–18uses Ricœur’s narrative/aporia inquiry in a comparison with Ginzburg. This specified resource coexists with disagreement over Aristotle;Hartog explicitly does not blame Ricœur for other historians’ unreflective deference. Original1983/1985/2000works unread.

edge_1941.relationship: Hartog uses Ginzburg’s reflections on narrative’s cognitive powers and the interaction of evidence and storytelling in comparing historical approaches to representation.
edge_1941.evidence_note: Own2011article read in2013Portuguese translation16–18 explicitly credits a realism that is not positivism and reconstructs Ginzburg’s narrative practice. It coexists with a later objection about Aristotle’s Rhetoric;not whole-program agreement or formative mentoring. Cited French2003Rapports de force and2010Le fil et les traces remain unread.

edge_1942.relationship: Hartog questions whether Ginzburg’s linkage of rhetoric and proof establishes Aristotle’s Rhetoric as the primary ancient account of historiography.
edge_1942.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article20–21 examines Thucydides’ reconstruction of the remote past and Aristotle’s placement of inquiries within political deliberation. Hartog grants the importance of proof and Ginzburg’s narrative sophistication;his objection is a particular ancient-text interpretation,not equating realism with positivism. Original Ginzburg works and Greek-text editions not freshly read beyond Hartog’s translated quotations.

edge_1943.relationship: Hartog argues that Ricœur’s extension of Aristotelian emplotment to historical narrative crosses the Poetics’ original separation of history from poetry.
edge_1943.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article21–22 calls this extension Ricœur’s philosophical right and recognizes his effort to preserve history’s referential intention through representance. It is a bounded interpretive disagreement,not accusation of fabrication or denial of Ricœur’s wider value. The negative effect of later historians’ deference is explicitly not assigned to Ricœur himself.

edge_1944.relationship: Hartog argues that White’s incorporation of historical poetics into rhetoric moves beyond Aristotle’s exclusion of history from poetic mimesis.
edge_1944.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article18–19 identifies the interpretive move while carefully distinguishing Ricœur’s and Ginzburg’s different readings of White. This is Hartog’s limited ancient/modern conceptual qualification,not wholesale rejection of narrative analysis or attribution of every anti-White argument to him. Metahistory and White’s complete corpus unread.

edge_1945.relationship: Hartog challenges the transhistorical authority claimed by Veyne’s invariant-based method and asks where the historian’s own discourse is produced.
edge_1945.evidence_note: Fresh1978primary essay read in Gustavo Ruiz Da Silva’s2025English translation,especially Without Concepts,You Don’t See Anything. It interrogates the relation of invariant models to progress in knowledge and likens classification to a herbarium. OriginalFrench326–327metadata/selectedOCR checked,but key329–330not obtained;no complete French-original reading claimed. Translator’s historical introduction/bracketed additions are distinct;Veyne’s1977lecture unread.

edge_1946.relationship: Hartog uses Foucault’s analysis of classical classification to develop his criticism of Veyne’s invariant method.
edge_1946.evidence_note: Own1978essay,read in2025translation,explicitly refers to Les mots et les choses together with François Jacob’s La logique du vivant as the source of the closing natural-history quotations and analogy. Jacob retains separate credit;they are two works,not coauthors. Neither original work nor its exact edition was freshly read;translator commentary is not used as Hartog’s argument.

edge_1947.relationship: Bederman explicitly credits Foucault’s discourse analysis with shaping her study of knowledge, material practice and power, while stressing contradiction and possible agency.
edge_1947.evidence_note: Own methodological declaration at printed24, followed by three specified uses of discourse analysis on24–25. Note97 identifies The History of Sexuality, vol.1 and Power/Knowledge; note29 also includes the former. No exclusive genealogy, agreement with every Foucauldian position or independent reading of Foucault’s originals. Note97 prints an unverified1972 date for Power/Knowledge; this is not silently adopted as an edition fact.

edge_1948.relationship: Bederman includes Butler’s Gender Trouble among the theoretical resources for treating gender as a historical process connecting bodies, identities and authority.
edge_1948.evidence_note: Body7 develops an ideological-process account; note29 directs readers first to Teresa de Lauretis and then, among plural resources, to Butler1990, Foucault1978, Denise Riley1988 and Scott1988/1992. A bounded, explicitly cited conceptual resource; not a claim of personal mentoring, sole derivation or full adoption. Original Gender Trouble unread.

edge_1951.relationship: Bederman draws on Ryan’s Cradle of the Middle Class to connect early middle-class formation, manly self-restraint and gendered family practices.
edge_1951.evidence_note: Body11–12 with notes38–40/43–44 explicitly supports these historical explanations. Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes is credited alongside Ryan; Blumin, Paul E. Johnson and Cott supply other aspects. No independent collation of Ryan1981 or wholesale adoption of her account.

edge_1952.relationship: Bederman uses Davidoff and Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes for the place of manliness and gendered family practices in middle-class formation.
edge_1952.evidence_note: Note38 expressly judges some observations from the English study applicable to the United States; body11–12 and notes40/42–43 use that joint work alongside Ryan, Cott and others. Both coauthors retain equal credit. This is a qualified transatlantic resource, not an assertion that English and American class formation were identical. Family Fortunes (1987) unread independently.

edge_1953.relationship: Bederman uses Davidoff and Hall’s jointly authored Family Fortunes for the place of manliness and gendered family practices in middle-class formation.
edge_1953.evidence_note: Note38 expressly judges some observations from the English study applicable to the United States; body11–12 and notes40/42–43 use that joint work alongside Ryan, Cott and others. Both coauthors retain equal credit. This is a qualified transatlantic resource, not an assertion that English and American class formation were identical. Family Fortunes (1987) unread independently.

edge_1954.relationship: Bederman uses Cott’s histories of womanhood and feminism in explaining gendered middle-class identity and challenges to established male authority.
edge_1954.evidence_note: Body11/n40 cites The Bonds of Womanhood (1977) alongside Ryan and jointly authored Davidoff/Hall;14/n53 cites The Grounding of Modern Feminism (1987) with Mari Jo Buhle and Filene. Note96 also points to Cott’s Two Beards (1990) as another discussion of civilization, without making that a personal formative claim. Cott originals unread.

edge_1955.relationship: Bederman uses Higham’s accounts of nativism and cultural reorientation as resources for connecting white middle-class manhood to immigrant politics and the appeal of boxing.
edge_1955.evidence_note: Body13/n50 links immigrant contests for city government to power and manhood, citing Strangers in the Land (1971 consulted edition) with Gossett. Body17/n72 cites Reorientation,78–79 for boxing’s wider middle-class attraction. This scoped use coexists with her criticism of a masculinity-crisis formulation; it is not evidence of complete agreement. Originals unread.

edge_1956.relationship: Bederman qualifies the masculinity-crisis interpretation represented in part by Higham, arguing that ongoing change and contradictory authority claims do not by themselves establish a crisis of male identity or power.
edge_1956.evidence_note: Body10–11 acknowledges merit in both crisis and domesticity interpretations, then distinguishes remaking gender from evidence that men lost confidence in male identity and authority. Note36 names Higham’s Reorientation alongside Dubbert, Filene, Kimmel and McGovern; note37 credits Marsh and Griffen’s corrective. A bounded collective criticism, not rejection of all Higham’s work; her separate uses of his nativism and boxing discussions remain.

edge_1957.relationship: Bederman uses Roediger’s Wages of Whiteness in explaining how white working men linked manly independence to exclusion of Black men.
edge_1957.evidence_note: Body20/n84 supports the specific contrast between white male claims to independence and exclusions shared by women and Black men. The note identifies Roediger1991; nearby Berthoff and Horton/Horton discussions have distinct claims. No independent reading of Wages of Whiteness or inference of personal affiliation.

edge_1959.relationship: Bederman includes Hofstadter’s Social Darwinism in American Thought among the historiographic resources for her account of Darwinism’s American reception and its tensions with Protestant millennial expectations.
edge_1959.evidence_note: Body26 describes educated Americans understanding Darwinism through conflict and survival without the older providential telos. Note102 directs readers to Hofstadter’s1955 edition alongside Robert C. Bannister1979 and Cynthia Eagle Russett1976 for Darwinism’s reception in the United States. This is a particular plural historical resource, not personal formation or wholesale adoption of Hofstadter’s interpretation. Originals unread. The separate self-employment statistic at12/n45 carries no additional interpretive claim.

edge_1962.relationship: Wood questions Greene’s concentration on conscious constitutional motives and later psychological explanations of the American Revolution.
edge_1962.evidence_note: Own1966 critique of neo-Whig historical explanation names Greene alongside Morgan, with necessary corrective credit retained. Own1982 opening identifies Greene’s Search for Identity1970 and Uneasy Connection1973 as examples of psychological readings that Wood seeks to replace with a wider account of eighteenth-century causal beliefs. Neither claim means every Greene interpretation was rejected.

edge_1964.relationship: Wood borrows Pocock’s formulation of a Namierian history of ideas to characterize Bailyn’s analysis of revolutionary thought.
edge_1964.evidence_note: Own1966 applies a specifically credited analytical formulation across the21–22 page break, n41 citing Pocock’s1965 articlep550. This is a small conceptual resource, not evidence that Wood adopted the whole later republican synthesis or a claim that Pocock coined every underlying idea. Pocock’s original article unread.

edge_1969.relationship: Wood questions Taylor’s treatment of captive violence and the narrative scale of The Divided Ground while praising its research and cultural analysis.
edge_1969.evidence_note: Own2006 review distinguishes omission criticism from praise of the murder-law analysis and research. Richter supplies Wood’s captive-treatment counterexample; the approved Richter→Wood resource is separately represented, not repeated. Richter’s unnamed study remains bibliographically unidentified. Taylor’s complete book and later2016/2021reviews unread; no general verdict on Native history adopted.

edge_1971.relationship: Wood uses Bailyn’s reconstruction of revolutionary ideas to frame a return to questions about their social sources.
edge_1971.evidence_note: Own1966pp20–24treats Bailyn’s1965Pamphlets introduction as a departure toward social explanation, rather than merely conscious motivation. This concrete use of a published interpretation differs from baseline edge1775’s1958seminar teaching influence; no second influence edge. Original1965introduction unread; later1967book/reprint annotations not projected into1966.

edge_1972.relationship: Wood invokes Arendt’s account of joint action to support his distinction between collective revolutionary processes and individual motives.
edge_1972.evidence_note: Own1966p23/n44adds Arendt, On Revolution(NewYork1963),p173 to a paragraph principally explaining Bailyn’s interpretation. Her specified collective-action argument reinforces the point; Bailyn retains the main interpretive credit. This is a bounded conceptual contribution, not formative influence or a reading of Arendt’s complete book. Original1963text unread.

edge_1973.relationship: Gellner uses Ibn Khaldun’s dynastic-cycle model to interpret the coexistence of tribal and urban power in Morocco.
edge_1973.evidence_note: Own1961review explicitly applies the analysis rather than merely praising a precursor. Alatas2006p789also identifies a later fusion with Hume in Gellner’s Muslim reform model; Hume retains separate credit, not an Ibn-only explanation. No precise Muqaddimah edition for Gellner’s1961reading is established; originalArabic and complete Muslim Society unread.

edge_1974.relationship: Malešević reports Gellner’s geographical qualification of Ibn Khaldun’s model to arid-zone tribal Islam.
edge_1974.evidence_note: Named mediation: Malešević2021p394attributes the regional limit and quotes Muslim Society1981p88. His own following argument about modern conditions is kept separate. Gellner’s admiration and application coexist with this qualification. Original1981page and whole book unread; no generalized rejection of Ibn Khaldun.

edge_1976.relationship: Gellner and Dale compare Ibn Khaldun with Durkheim on social cohesion and the explanatory study of society, retaining differences in context and normative aims.
edge_1976.evidence_note: Gellner’s1975opening extract and Dale’s2006pp442–444supply distinct comparisons. Dale emphasizes shared logical methods and divergent historical conditions. This is their comparison; no direct transmission or medieval membership in modern sociology inferred. Full Durkheim works unread.

edge_1977.relationship: Dale compares Ibn Khaldun and Bloch on cohesion, comparison and testing historical reports, while distinguishing Bloch’s attention to individual motives.
edge_1977.evidence_note: Dale2006pp444–445reads Feudal Society and Historian’s Craft comparatively. Shared analytical questions do not establish direct reading or descent. Dale qualifies the analogy; complete Bloch works and underlying editions unread here.

edge_1979.relationship: Dale reports White’s concern that Ibn Khaldun’s structural explanation can subordinate human action to underlying regularities.
edge_1979.evidence_note: Mediated narrowly through Dale2006p444and450n92, which attributes the antihumanistic assessment of Ibn Khaldun to White’s1959review. Dale’s broader comparison is his own. Original review body unavailable; publisher extract/metadata only checked, including Rosenthal1958translation reviewed. No claim to reproduce White’s full evaluation or his later narrative theory.

edge_1983.relationship: Uses Hofstadter’s bill-of-lading characterization as a rhetorical foil in discussing the Emancipation Proclamation.
edge_1983.evidence_note: Own scanned1996 essay30 reuses the attributed description;2001 Q&A qualifies its implication by emphasizing extraordinary effects despite flat wording. The speech calls it moral impact, whereas scanned essay says moral grandeur; do not silently merge as a verified original quotation. Original Hofstadter passage unread. This resource does not imply agreement that proclamation lacked political force.

edge_1984.relationship: Identifies Davis’s slavery studies as guides to slavery’s double status as property and person and to abolition in the age of capitalism.
edge_1984.evidence_note: Explicit authorial Prologue notes5–6 in displayed digital selection, with Hegel credited first in note5. Western Culture1966 and Age of Revolution1975 have distinct purposes. No direct first-edition collation or complete Prologue/book reading, and no general mentorship or causal debt inferred.

edge_1985.relationship: Identifies Roll, Jordan, Roll as the starting point for the contemporary debate on master-slave paternalism.
edge_1985.evidence_note: Explicit evaluative authorial note6 in displayed digital notes; a resource for a debate, not assent to all of Genovese’s conclusions. Coexists with Berlin’s particular2003 chronological-scope criticism.1974 title/year are as cited by Berlin; the2001 speech reading list uses a different1976 edition. Both original editions and full Berlin Prologue unread.

edge_1987.relationship: Questions the limited attention to slavery before1830 in Genovese’s nineteenth-century-centered historiography.
edge_1987.evidence_note: Only the fresh publisher opening extract of Berlin2003 article read. He groups Genovese with Kenneth Stampp, Stanley Elkins, John Blassingame, Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman and acknowledges their sharp disagreements. Do not infer rejection of paternalism, statistics or Marxism from this temporal-scope criticism; complete article and underlying books unread.

edge_1988.relationship: Defends the regional and chronological scope of Slaves Without Masters against Ely’s reported charge that Berlin equates restrictive law with daily life.
edge_1988.evidence_note: Own2004 Foner review permits generalizations, regional comparisons and change over1790–1860 that a single-county study cannot provide, while valuing Ely’s local research. This is an explicitly bounded reception intervention; it neither certifies all Berlin findings nor credits Berlin with writing Foner’s reply. Original books unread.

edge_1989.relationship: Supplies Roediger with a formulation making African American family history central to the history of the working class.
edge_1989.evidence_note: Selected indexed own1993 paragraph128 expressly quotes Berlin’s1987 Gutman introduction46. Berlin mediates Gutman’s research agenda; note2 co-credits Montgomery/Gutman/Rawick interviews and retains Brody’s range-of-positions qualification. Not a claim Berlin founded Roediger’s full argument; complete article and Berlin’s original introduction unread.

edge_1991.relationship: As Megan Hamilton reads the1999 response, Palmer contests Granatstein’s picture of a declining historical profession while also questioning the defensive self-satisfaction of its critics.
edge_1991.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Hamilton2021,28/notes44–45 identifies Palmer’s argument that historians are doing well and that defensive reaction to Granatstein has displaced critical reflection. The response is also directed at McKillop; Palmer is not flattened into McKillop’s camp. Original Palmer1999CHR80:4,676–686 and Granatstein’s1998book remain unread. Hamilton’s printed journal essay is a student scholarly publication, not treated as a direct reading of either original or as proof of every Palmer argument.

edge_1992.relationship: Buckner contrasts Granatstein’s sweeping fragmentation charge with Owram’s more qualified pursuit of national synthesis that retains the value of recent social history.
edge_1992.evidence_note: Own fresh reading of Buckner2000,9: he explicitly groups their fragmentation diagnoses but distinguishes Owram’s willingness to take the last30years of scholarship seriously and his acceptance of social history. Buckner himself contests both the hierarchy of national versus subdisciplinary history and the premise that regional history fragments Canada. An attributed comparison, not an Owram attack on Granatstein or an intellectual transmission. Granatstein1998 and Owram1997 original bodies unread.

edge_1993.relationship: Greene qualifies Anderson’s account of intercolonial connections and challenges what he reads as an insufficiently lived and materially grounded account of corporate identity.
edge_1993.evidence_note: Own2019answer explicitly accepts some mercantile links and the importance of Spanish imperial geography, but stresses competitive/local political identities and stronger transatlantic ties in other colonies. He then argues that corporate identities arise through economic practice, custom and legal culture. The suggestion that Anderson makes identity merely imaginary is Greene’s characterization, not certified here as a faithful account of Imagined Communities. Interviewer framing is distinct; Anderson1983original unread.

edge_1996.relationship: Greene qualifies Wood’s case for the Revolution’s radicalism by treating the later change in civic language as gradual, facilitated by independence and possibly achievable without it.
edge_1996.evidence_note: Own2019answer grants the opening for new ways of talking about ordinary people and politics, then stresses a roughly fifty-year transition rather than an immediately radical event. His subsequent comparison emphasizes centralization in France and continuing composite authority in the United States. Friendship does not erase the disagreement. Wood’s complete books and R.R.Palmer’s1959work unread; Palmer is introduced by the interviewer. The reverse Wood→Greene critique and Greene→Wood contribution are already queued in Wood’s accepted packet, not duplicated here.

edge_1997.relationship: Lears identifies Gramsci’s account of cultural hegemony as a framework for rethinking power, consent and cultural meaning in American history.
edge_1997.evidence_note: Own1985explicitly adopts a framework and vocabulary while declining an uncritical embrace of the revolutionary program. Hoare/Nowell Smith’s1971Prison Notebooks translation and Lawner’s1973Letters are specified witnesses, not the complete Italian corpus. Own2010recollection retains Genovese and Davis as interpreters in his graduate intellectual environment.

edge_1999.relationship: Lears invokes Thompson’s unintended-consequences formulation and his account of law’s relative autonomy when explaining cultural meaning and power.
edge_1999.evidence_note: Own Cohen answer expressly paraphrases Thompson, without establishing the original aphorism’s exact wording or source. Own1985p590uses Whigs and Hunters1975pp258–269 among plural models for ideology’s promise. Specific resources, not a claim to adopt all Thompson.

edge_2000.relationship: Lears uses Williams’s account of feeling and cultural relations when developing a less mechanical conception of hegemony.
edge_2000.evidence_note: Own1985invokes structure of feeling and identifies a parallel base/superstructure argument;1973article and The Long Revolution1961pp48–71 are distinct cited works. This is Raymond, not Eric Williams. Complete originals unread.

edge_2001.relationship: Lears uses Genovese’s account of paternalism, accommodation and resistance to develop a historical analysis of hegemony.
edge_2001.evidence_note: Own1985draws on Roll, Jordan, Roll1974pp585–665 and separately In Red and Black1970p369. He explicitly says his summary simplifies a complex argument; slaves’ dignity and resistance remain alongside accommodation. Whole books unread.

edge_2002.relationship: Lears questions the classification of slave protest as prepolitical and the risk of making planter hegemony too static.
edge_2002.evidence_note: Own578parenthesis places Genovese’s formulation beside Gramsci’s teleological limits;586reports criticism of a monolithic planter image while crediting Genovese’s sensitivity. It coexists with substantive use, not rejection of Roll, Jordan, Roll as a whole.

edge_2003.relationship: Lears uses Hofstadter’s critique of the entrepreneurial consensus to frame how dissent can share dominant cultural commitments.
edge_2003.evidence_note: Own576praises analytical insight but expressly denies making Hofstadter a Gramscian after the fact. The American Political Tradition1948 is cited atn19; the distinct Populism criticism concerns Age of Reform1955. Originals unread.

edge_2005.relationship: Lears uses Davis’s analysis of abolitionism’s unintended consequences to extend hegemony beyond deliberate social control.
edge_2005.evidence_note: Own588/n50credits The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution1974pp349–350, then extends the problem to private psychic needs. Robert Merton retains earlier general formulation credit. This is Lears’s use of a contested interpretation, not independent confirmation of Davis’s entire thesis. His2010mentor recollection is supplementary.

edge_2006.relationship: Lears uses Foner’s account of artisans and price controls to show contradictions within producer ideology.
edge_2006.evidence_note: Own575locates the shift from communal moral economy toward entrepreneurial expectations in Foner’s research. Plural surrounding reconstruction includes Laurie, Dawley, Hahn and Wilentz. Cited Tom Paine and Revolutionary America1976pp41,157 and chapter5; complete original unread.

edge_2007.relationship: Lears invokes Woodward’s account of political coercion and fraud as necessary context for explaining Populism’s defeat.
edge_2007.evidence_note: Own576credits Origins of the New South1877–1913(1951) while extending the analysis through Goodwyn’s cultural account. Political coercion is not replaced by an exclusively symbolic explanation. Complete original unread.

edge_2008.relationship: Lears uses Weber’s treatment of hypothetical nonoccurrences to frame inquiry into unrealized historical possibilities.
edge_2008.evidence_note: Own585/n44specifies Critical Studies in the Logic of the Cultural Sciences in Shils/Finch1949Methodology of the Social Sciences,164–188. This methodological resource is distinct from loose Weberian-modernity language in the Serlin interview. LaCapra/Heidegger retain separate credit for thinking the unthought. Complete cited original unread.

edge_2009.relationship: Lears draws on Bourdieu’s work on education and taste as a model for investigating cultural reproduction.
edge_2009.evidence_note: Own589credits Bourdieu while insisting that actual audience/student experience remains to be studied. Reproduction is jointly authored with J.C.Passeron(cited1977edition); Distinction is cited in Richard Nice’s1984translation. These are plural methodological resources, not verified complete readings here.

edge_2010.relationship: Lears questions how Geertzian cultural analysis can obscure unequal power and larger political-economic structures.
edge_2010.evidence_note: Own573criticizes both an implicit functionalism and historians’ uses of symbolic systems. Own586–587credits Rhys Isaac with overcoming that limitation rather than treating all Geertz-inspired history as defective. Original Geertz1973collection unread.

edge_2011.relationship: Lears questions antisubjectivist readings of Foucault and their capacity to explain agency and a shared political good.
edge_2011.evidence_note: Own1985recognizes salutary effects of socially constituted subjectivity before objecting to mechanistic agency-denial. Own2010distinguishes Foucault’s useful surveillance analysis from an individualist academic reception; it is not a claim that every recipient interpretation is Foucault’s own doctrine. Cited original books unread.

edge_2012.relationship: Lears uses White’s account of semiotic codes to ask how discourse establishes plausibility beyond fixed ideological binaries.
edge_2012.evidence_note: Own590adopts the question while reserving criticism of White’s subsequent Adams reading. Cited1982essay Method and Ideology in Intellectual History, in LaCapra/Kaplan edited Modern European Intellectual History,288–289; original essay unread.

edge_2013.relationship: Lears questions White’s emphasis on nihilism in Henry Adams, arguing that it overlooks vitalism, religious longing and Marian Adams.
edge_2013.evidence_note: Own593/n62singles out a particular reading, credits its skill and distinguishes it from the useful semiotic questions adopted earlier. White’s1982essay290–310 and Adams’s full Education unread here; no verdict on all White’s narrative theory.

edge_2014.relationship: Lears uses Lefebvre’s concern about depleted signs in consumer culture to question celebratory accounts of struggles over meaning.
edge_2014.evidence_note: Own592gives plural credit to Lefebvre, Baudrillard and William Leiss, with Stephen Kline jointly credited in one cited study. Lefebvre source is Everyday Life in the Modern World, Sacha Rabinovitch translation1971p119. No entire translated book read.

edge_2015.relationship: Lears questions the historical usefulness of Habermas’s ideal speech situation as a possible alternative to hegemonic discourse.
edge_2015.evidence_note: Own585regards completely undistorted communication as too remote for this historical task, then proposes inquiry into nearer unrealized possibilities. Cites What Is Universal Pragmatics? in Communication and the Evolution of Society, Thomas McCarthy translation1979p63. This is a task-specific limitation, not rejection of all Habermas; original unread.

edge_2017.relationship: Lears uses Hall and the Birmingham Centre’s reciprocal model of cultural meaning before qualifying its account of subcultural resistance.
edge_2017.evidence_note: Own590names Hall and colleagues;591n56cites both a Centre collection and Resistance through Rituals, jointly edited by Hall and Tony Jefferson(cited1975). Hall is not sole author of every case study. The example supplies a point of departure, not uncritical endorsement; originals unread.

edge_2018.relationship: Lears questions whether Hall and Birmingham’s bricolage framework sufficiently explains the character of youth resistance.
edge_2018.evidence_note: Own590–591moves from the named Hall/collective account of Teddy Boys to the objection that celebration alone is insufficient, then proposes Bakhtin’s multivalence. Collective authors and coeditor Tony Jefferson retain credit; no claim that all Hall writing celebrates consumption.

edge_2019.relationship: McKay adopts and extends Lears’s definition of antimodernism when explaining the construction of Scottish Nova Scotia.
edge_2019.evidence_note: Own McKay1992p9/n12quotes No Place of Grace1981p xv and adds simple life and nature. Personal resource is demonstrated by this use, not co-citation. Existing edge895is a McKay→Canadian field contribution; no duplicate field edge or inference that all Quest of the Folk1994was read. Lears’s original book remains unread.

edge_2021.relationship: Lears uses deconstructionist attention to intertextuality and multiple meanings as a resource for moving beyond binary cultural interpretations.

karl.label: Historical materialism
karl.date_label: Marx’s preface 1859 · Capital I 1867 · later Marxists
karl.description: Modes of production, relations of exploitation, class struggle, and historically specific capitalism. Later Marxists disagree over determinism, agency, and culture. Marx’s 1859 developmental propositions coexist with his 1877 rejection of a universal path. Later debates concern political action, imperial accumulation, dialectical and analytical explanation, and reproduction of material life.
karl.representative_figures_and_works: Karl Marx (1818–1883), Capital I (1867); developed in critical engagement with political economy, philosophy, and socialist movements.

representative_people.context: Analyzes historically specific production and exploitation. The 1859 preface advances strong forces/relations propositions; the 1877 Russian letter rejects exporting the Western-European expropriation account as a universal path. These claims require comparison, not silent harmonization.
representative_people.works: Capital I (1867); preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859); Russian editorial-board letter (1877)

representative_people.context: A specific historical use of capitalism, wage labor and family dependence to explain sexual identity; not an assertion of formal school membership or a universal cause.

historicalecon.label: Historical economics
historicalecon.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction. Earlier disputes also separate Jones’s comparative tenures, Roscher’s contextual programme, Hildebrand’s critique of opposed specialization schemes and Knies’s objections to Roscher’s method. Leslie’s account emphasizes policy differences within historical inquiry.
historicalecon.representative_figures_and_works: Gustav Schmoller; William Ashley; William Cunningham; Arnold Toynbee. Thorold Rogers supplies a related empirical tradition in prices and wages. Contextual readings now distinguish Roscher’s 1843 programme, Schmoller’s 1883 methodological review, Cunningham’s textbook, Ashley’s medieval studies, Toynbee’s lectures, Rogers’s wage research and Menger’s criticism.

historicalecon.scope_note: German historical economics, British institutional history, and empirical price studies overlap without forming one school. Roscher’s earlier programme and Schmoller’s generation differ. Menger is shown as a critic, and Toynbee explicitly rejects exclusive reliance on historical investigation. National and civilizational categories in these texts are historical claims to examine, not a globally representative framework. Jones’s providential harmony and Hildebrand’s national-capacity judgments are not adopted as findings.

economictheory.label: Political economy & economic theory
economictheory.date_label: Smith 1776 · Ricardo 1817 · Mill 1848 · Marshall 1890 · later adaptations
economictheory.description: A contested body of explanation about production, distribution and exchange. Smith’s division of labour, Ricardo’s distribution problem, Mill’s institutional distinctions, Marshall’s treatment of markets and time, and Menger’s account of theory offer different resources. Historians adapt and criticize these arguments rather than inheriting one uniform model.
economictheory.representative_figures_and_works: Adam Smith is an eighteenth-century precursor; Ricardo, Mill, and Marshall represent different nineteenth-century developments. This is not a single unchanging paradigm. Read Smith (1776), Ricardo (1817/1821), Mill (1848), Marshall (1890/1920), and Menger’s methodological intervention (1883) as differing arguments, not a linear succession.

economictheory.scope_note: Classical political economy and neoclassical modelling have different chronologies; North’s later institutional revisions add another distinction. This selection foregrounds earlier resources for historical inquiry, not a complete history of twentieth-century economics. Mill’s institutional argument and Marshall’s qualified assumptions prevent a blanket equation of theory with timeless laws. Polanyi appears as a later critic of a specific classical account, extending the selection’s historical reception without turning it into a complete history of twentieth-century theory. Earlier resources remain central, now joined by selected twentieth-century historical uses: Furtado’s Keynes reference, Block/Somers’s Polanyi reception and Lipset’s Schumpeter definition. These do not constitute comprehensive coverage of modern economics. Mill’s property qualifications coexist with colonial and civilizational assumptions; Marx’s Wakefield critique also retains a settler frame. Naoroji adds an Indian appropriation of Mill, not a globally representative roster.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Richard White, Railroaded (2011): corporate finance, public subsidies and political markets; selected author interview passages checked. N. F. R. Crafts and C. K. Harley, “Output Growth and the British Industrial Revolution” (1992), restatement checked through its abstract.

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

representative_people.works: L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution (1856), Avant-propos 5–12

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Archives, government and religious authority
strands.focus: Ranke’s church/state inquiry and Cam’s medieval local institutions use historical records for different political problems; neither alone founded all source criticism.
strands.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836); Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944)

strands.title: Parliamentary connections and collective biography
strands.focus: Reconstruct actors’ social and political connections; the institutional focus raises questions about ideology and people excluded from parliamentary participation.
strands.works: The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (1929)

strands.title: Voters and competing group explanations
strands.focus: Benson tests class-centered interpretations against ethnic and religious voting patterns in New York; this is a local historical argument, not a universal electoral rule.

strands.title: Radical ideas and popular political action
strands.focus: Compare religious radicalism, Chartist participation and colonial peasant insurgency without making one a derivative instance of another.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); The Chartists (1984); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders. Scott’s studies of French feminists and the parity movement, known through her reviewers, examine claims to inclusion caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference.

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

quant.label: Quantitative history
quant.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.
quant.representative_figures_and_works: Historical demography; Robert Fogel and Douglass North in cliometrics. Further selections: Labrousse (1933), Benson (1961), Thernstrom (1964), Curtin (1969), Fogel and Engerman (1974), Gutman’s critique (1975).

representative_people.context: Uses explicit counterfactuals to question the indispensability of railroads; his collaboration on slavery provoked criticism of its evidence and interpretation. Later population/health research is a separate programme.
representative_people.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); with Stanley Engerman, Time on the Cross (1974); Nobel lecture (1993)

representative_people.context: Economic historian whose institutional explanation examines rules, incentives, learning and historical paths; later work revises assumptions associated with earlier neoclassical analysis.
representative_people.works: “Economic Performance through Time” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Differential movements of prices, production and income support conjunctural inquiry. His 1956 introduction stresses uneven crises; later debate tests the model’s conditions and distinguishes his experiments from serial routines.
representative_people.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956)

strands.title: Serial evidence and collective patterns
strands.focus: Prices and incomes support conjunctural and social questions without requiring neoclassical theory.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933)

strands.title: Population reconstruction
strands.focus: Family linkage and aggregate reconstruction differ in units and assumptions; missing mobile families are a methodological problem Henry explicitly identifies.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); The Population History of England (1981)

strands.title: Cliometrics
strands.focus: Fogel’s counterfactual railroad comparison and North’s institutional development are different uses of economic reasoning; neither stands for all quantitative history.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Electoral groups and competing explanations
strands.focus: Compare economic interests with ethnic and religious affiliations in New York voting; Benson’s categories overlap and his argument is not a universal law of elections.

strands.title: Occupations, property and social mobility
strands.focus: Separate occupational change from property accumulation through linked local records; Thernstrom’s use of Weber broadens class beyond a single occupational ranking.

strands.title: Slavery: estimates, coercion and interpretation
strands.focus: Read the cliometric study alongside Gutman’s criticism of its labor/cooperation interpretation; neither efficiency estimates nor a book’s polemical reception alone describe enslaved people’s lives.
strands.works: Time on the Cross (1974); Slavery and the Numbers Game (1975)

strands.title: Estimating the Atlantic slave trade
strands.focus: Reconstruct the scale of forced migration from uneven evidence. Curtin’s influential estimates were later revised; totals do not substitute for histories of violence and agency.
strands.works: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

strands.title: Household surveys and the limits of response
strands.focus: Salmon combines employer and worker returns, bureau tabulation and wage comparisons. Distribution through college and association networks, reluctance to reply and uneven knowledge qualify her representativeness claims.

strands.title: Counterfactual assumptions and sensitivity
strands.focus: McClelland’s criticism makes alternative transport capacity, pricing and cost assumptions explicit questions. Critiquing a model’s inference is itself quantitative historical work.

strands.title: Revenue and technical efficiency
strands.focus: David and Temin distinguish revenue from producing the same outputs with fewer inputs. Their specific objection should be read with the authors’ reply; the reply is located here, but its body remains unchecked.

strands.title: Who remains visible in mobility records?
strands.focus: Ferrie questions findings based on local stayers and late observation after arrival. Linking migrants expands observation, but selective linkage and occupational coding still constrain inference.

strands.title: Caste, occupation and colonial counts
strands.focus: Kumar states the assumptions needed to estimate earlier agricultural labour from later caste counts. Changing census categories and officials’ conflation of caste with occupation limit comparison.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts IV,X

strands.title: Sampling parishes and their surviving records
strands.focus: The Fleury–Henry programme requires more than a collection of convenient local studies. Its later implementation changes sampling to meet practical constraints and treats earlier, poorer records separately.

strands.title: Fertility measures and their denominators
strands.focus: Lee and Wang distinguish synthetic total fertility from fertility within marriage and state adjustments to several underlying estimates. Interpreting those measures requires more than comparing the resulting totals.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999), Table6.1 notes and86–90

quant.scope_note: Serial history, demographic reconstruction, and cliometrics use numbers differently. A quantitative method does not establish a common theory. Counting, source linkage and formal modeling require different assumptions. Recorded categories, missing people and units of comparison shape conclusions; neither criticism nor narrative history ended quantitative research.

language.label: Linguistic turn / poststructuralism
language.description: Examines how language, narrative, discourse, and power shape historical knowledge and subject formation. Narrative theory, structuralist inheritances, and poststructuralist critiques overlap but are not interchangeable. This node groups debates rather than identifying one school.
language.representative_figures_and_works: Michel Foucault; Jacques Derrida; Hayden White, Metahistory (1973). Richard Rorty, ed.: The Linguistic Turn (1967).

representative_people.context: Discourse, genealogy and subject formation are related, changing inquiries; institutional and practical relations enter the account. Historians adapt and criticize them in different ways.
representative_people.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971); “The Subject and Power” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions conceptual hierarchies and conditions of signification through close reading and institutional questions; no mechanical rule permits arbitrary interpretation.
representative_people.works: Of Grammatology (1967); “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

representative_people.context: Historical narrative theory; not every position under the linguistic turn.
representative_people.works: Metahistory (1973); The Content of the Form (1987); Figural Realism (1999); The Practical Past (2014)

representative_people.context: Reworks signification and unconscious interpretation; the linguistic turn is not a uniform Lacanian program.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Écrits collection (1966)

representative_people.context: Theorizes material ideology and the constitution of subjects; reception is specifically documented through Hall and cultural-studies debates.
representative_people.works: “Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses” (1970); Hall, “Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms” (1980)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor in historians’ reception of Foucault, organizing debate across theoretical and empirical approaches. The edited volume is not one uniform Foucauldian program.
representative_people.works: Foucault and the Writing of History, edited collection (1994); Console and Classify (1987)

representative_people.context: Derrida examines the relation of writing to the historicity of ideal objects through Husserl’s geometry. This is a particular critical engagement, not Husserl’s membership in a later historical turn.
representative_people.works: Husserl’s Origin of Geometry as discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), chapter 2 opening

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly identifies Destruktion and Abbau as resources that he adapts; the acknowledgment does not imply endorsement of Heidegger’s whole philosophy or politics.
representative_people.works: Derrida, “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly draws on signs and interpretants while questioning a final meaning outside signification. This contextual use does not equate pragmatism with deconstruction.

representative_people.context: An explicit resource in Foucault’s genealogy and Barthes’s discussion of facts and meaning; their appropriations are distinct from Nietzsche’s full argument.
representative_people.works: Genealogy (1887), selected passages; Foucault’s genealogy essay (1971); Barthes’s history essay (1967)

representative_people.works: Mythologies (1957); “The Discourse of History” and “The Death of the Author” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Barthes invokes his research on ambiguous words in Greek tragedy to distinguish characters’ understanding from the spectator’s. This is a named scholarly resource, not a formal linguistic-turn affiliation.

representative_people.context: A historian and translator who makes rhetorical analysis usable for historiography while retaining questions about sources and reference.

strands.title: Discourse and genealogy
strands.focus: Archaeology examines rules connecting actual statements and the formation of objects; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Social and institutional relations enter these inquiries.
strands.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), three chapters; “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971), pp. 139–152

strands.title: Deconstruction
strands.focus: Critical work through conceptual hierarchies and differential relations, with an explicitly adapted Heidegger resource. The 1983 letter rejects a mechanical method and includes institutions and translation.
strands.works: Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2; “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983)

strands.title: Narrative theory
strands.focus: Emplotment and tropes concern the forms of historical explanation.

strands.title: Signification and divided subjectivity
strands.focus: Lacan’s changed sign diagram and reading of dream-work distinguish his appropriation from literal repetition of Saussure. Historians debate its capacity to explain changing gender relations.

strands.title: Ideology, practices and subjects
strands.focus: Althusser’s interpellation operates through material practices. His apparatuses include contradiction and resistance; Hall’s adoption and criticism remain a specific reception.

strands.title: Subject formation, action and resistance
strands.focus: Foucault distinguishes power relations from capacities and communication while studying their interconnections; freedom and resistance enter action upon actions. Goldstein provides a historically situated interlocutor.
strands.works: “The Subject and Power” (1982); Foucault and the Writing of History (1994)

strands.title: Writing, ideal objects and historicity
strands.focus: Derrida’s critical reading of Husserl asks how writing enters the historical transmission of ideal objects. It is distinct from a claim that historical evidence has no constraints.

strands.title: Interpretants and a critique of presence
strands.focus: Peirce is a named resource in Derrida’s account of signification; this particular use neither subsumes all pragmatism nor equates arbitrariness with individual caprice.
strands.works: Of Grammatology, corrected English edition (1997), pp. 44–50

strands.title: Madness, reason and discursive practice
strands.focus: Derrida questions the language of an archaeology of silence; Foucault disputes his reading of Descartes and the reduction of discursive practices to textual traces. Each criticism remains attributed.
strands.works: “Cogito and the History of Madness” (lecture 1963); “My Body, This Paper, This Fire” (English 1979)

strands.title: Genealogical questions and perspectival knowledge
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s distinction between origins and uses, and his account of multiple perspectives, enter different later arguments in Foucault and Barthes. Their readings are not interchangeable.
strands.works: Genealogy II.12–13 and III.12; Foucault (1971); Barthes (1967)

strands.title: Myth and the naturalization of history
strands.focus: Barthes’s two-level account asks how historically produced meanings appear natural. He links formal analysis with historical criticism, rather than treating semiology as sufficient by itself.

strands.title: Authorship, textual plurality and the reader
strands.focus: The 1967 essay questions the author as final explanatory authority and invokes Vernant’s tragic ambiguity. Its theoretical reader must be distinguished from research on actual readers.
strands.works: “The Death of the Author” (1967), Richard Howard translation

strands.title: Historical utterance, reference and narrative detail
strands.focus: Barthes distinguishes acts of uttering, content units and signification, drawing on Jakobson and Kristeva. Bann’s adoption and qualification keep historical practice within the debate.
strands.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: Social sites and textual action
strands.focus: Spiegel combines attention to form with documentary and patronage inquiry; texts act in social settings and are not transparent reflections.

strands.title: Gender categories and historical experience
strands.focus: Scott makes experience something to explain and connects meanings with institutions and subjectivity.

strands.title: Class and political idioms
strands.focus: Different historical inquiries question how social identities receive political meaning: Stedman Jones's study of grievance 'within political languages themselves' (1983, as quoted by Foster), Joyce's 'family of populisms' (1991), Vernon's popular constitutionalism and civic landscapes 'read as cultural texts' (1993, as quoted by Tilly), and Lawrence's insistence that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches be combined (2010). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); Visions of the People (1991); Politics and the People (1993); Speaking for the People (1998)

strands.title: Texts, contexts and debates over experience
strands.focus: LaCapra’s textual/contextual project and Toews’s explicitly titled meaning/experience intervention are distinct; detailed agreement is not presumed.

strands.title: Literary taxonomies and historical events
strands.focus: White distinguishes narrative arrangement from invented events and treats plot classifications as revisable analytical choices.

environment.label: Environmental history
environment.date_label: 1970s consolidation · Environmental History (journal) 1996 · NiCHE 2004 · Canadian number of Environmental History 2007 · Sutter forum 2013 · Oxford Handbook 2014 · reviewed through 2024
environment.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature; the approaches disagree about causal emphasis, and cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecology with power without one model. Bullard and the Huggins life histories add unequal burdens and authority over accounts; the Dust Bowl debates set capitalism, technology, policy and survival against one another. After 1995 the field argued with itself and its neighbours: Cronon called wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'; Foreman answered that this 'Received Wilderness Idea is a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (2000); Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks. A merged journal (1996), McNeill's world synthesis (2000) and a Canadian network (NiCHE, 2004) widened it; by 2013 Sutter found nature and culture replaced by 'environmental hybridity' (editors' summary). Chakrabarty (2009) and the Anthropocene histories of 2016 set its questions at planetary scale.
environment.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history. After 2000: J. R. McNeill, Something New Under the Sun (2000) and 'Observations' (2003); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Sutter, 'The World with Us' (JAH 2013); Isenberg, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Environmental History (2014); in Canada, Wynn (series editor), MacEachern, Loo, Piper, Sandlos, Evenden, Colpitts, Parr; the Anthropocene: Chakrabarty (2009), McNeill and Engelke, Malm, Bonneuil and Fressoz (2016). Institutions: Environmental History (journal, 1996), NiCHE (2004).
