environment.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community. Extended to 2024 on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md). Read in full: Foreman's 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000), Cronon's CV and 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003), the NiCHE and UBC Press series pages, publisher pages and abstracts for the Canadian books and articles, two open reviews of Worster's Shrinking the Earth; passages read: Cronon's 'Storytelling' (2013) and McNeill's AHA address (2020). Unread: the 1996 comments by Hays, Cohen and Dunlap and Cronon's response; Sutter's 2013 essay and its six responses (the editors' summary is quoted instead); McNeill 2000 and 2003 (the latter known from the earlier record); the 2005 'What's Next' forum including Linda Nash on agency; the bodies of every Canadian book; Malm, Moore, Bonneuil and Fressoz beyond descriptions. The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 dates the field's readership: 1.6% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of its authors in the 1990s, 5.7% in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25; the network of works co-cited with its founders (Cronon's Changes, Nature's Metropolis and 'The Trouble with Wilderness'; Worster's Dust Bowl, Rivers of Empire and Nature's Economy; White's Organic Machine; Crosby's Ecological Imperialism; Merchant's Death of Nature; works with lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 (37 works) and halved by 2020–25 (17), its new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; in the US it is stable (17–19 works) and its entrants are Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. The History PhD citation graph interprets these sampled co-citation neighbourhoods as diffusion into neighbouring historiographies. This does not establish declining scholarly production or the field's own understanding of its development.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.
strands.works: “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995; journal reprint with comments and a response, Environmental History 1:1, January 1996)

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.

strands.title: Material change, ideas and gendered nature
strands.focus: Merchant retrospectively clarifies that ecological and economic changes made some ideas more plausible rather than mechanically causing them. Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction and challenges an essentialist identification of women with nature.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); Radical Ecology (1992), discussed in Merchant’s 2006 retrospective

strands.title: Colonial conservation: knowledge, power and benefits
strands.focus: Carruthers’s review welcomes Grove’s island settings and exchanges of knowledge, while questioning parts of his synthesis. Her Kruger prologue and epilogue emphasize changing political coalitions, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Scientific conservation and unequal power can coexist; these works ask different questions at different scales.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

strands.title: The wilderness debate, 1995–2000: a selected exchange
strands.focus: Cronon's essay (1995; reprinted with comments in the first number of Environmental History, January 1996) held wilderness to be 'quite profoundly a human creation' and 'a flight from history' while defending wild-land protection. Hays replied in the journal that 'Cronon's wilderness is a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (as quoted by Foreman; comment unread). Sessions objected from conservation biology (1996). Callicott and Nelson gathered thirty-nine essays as The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998), where Foreman's 'Wilderness Areas for Real' answered. Foreman then told a federal wilderness-science conference (1999; printed 2000) that he came 'not to praise The Received Wilderness Idea, but to bury it': the idea that 'Baird Callicott, Bill Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars so eagerly banish' was 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground', unlike 'the Real Wilderness Idea' that built the National Wilderness Preservation System. A selected exchange: Cohen's and Dunlap's comments, the editors' introduction to the anthology and Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) are unread; in 2003 he answered in practice, asking that the Apostle Islands be managed 'as a historical wilderness' — 'Emphatically yes' to designation, but 'a storied wilderness'.
strands.works: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995; Environmental History 1:1, 1996, with comments and a response); Callicott and Nelson, eds., The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998); Foreman, 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000); Cronon, 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003)

strands.title: The Anthropocene and the climate of history
strands.focus: Chakrabarty's four theses (2009) held that anthropogenic climate change collapses the distinction between natural and human history (edge_918; critics at edge_1147). Environmental historians then wrote the epoch: McNeill and Engelke's The Great Acceleration (2016) says 'The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene' and that 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated' it; Malm's Fossil Capital (2016) answers that 'steam offered neither cheaper nor more abundant energy' but control over labour, against what a reviewer on its cover calls the 'Anthropocene narrative'; Bonneuil and Fressoz refuse 'the convenient view of a "human species" that upset the Earth system, unaware of what it was doing' (publisher descriptions; bodies unread). Worster's Shrinking the Earth (2016) was read by Collomb as 'reflections of the greatest US environmental historian on humankind's future and the Anthropocene'. McNeill told the AHA (2020) that 'environmental history stands to be disrupted, and with luck enhanced, more than most fields'. In PhD bibliographies this is a strand of the historiography, not of reading: Chakrabarty is cited by 4.5% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, in three families (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).
strands.works: Chakrabarty, 'The Climate of History' (2009); McNeill and Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016); Malm, Fossil Capital (2016); Bonneuil and Fressoz, The Shock of the Anthropocene (2016); Worster, Shrinking the Earth (2016)

strands.title: Canadian environmental history: a network and a series, 2001–2019
strands.focus: Wynn (2003) found the field 'undeveloped in this country, compared with the United States'. Within a decade it had institutions: NiCHE, 'founded in fall 2004 by a small team of scholars' and funded by a SSHRC Strategic Knowledge Cluster grant from 2007 (MacEachern director; Wynn, Turkel, Castonguay, Evenden and Piper on the executive); Wynn's UBC Press series Nature | History | Society, 'devoted to the publication of high-quality scholarship in environmental history and allied fields'; and a Canadian number of Environmental History (October 2007, edited by Evenden and MacEachern) in which Piper and Sandlos found that 'the Canadian North was never subject to the broad ecological transformation that occurred further to the south' and Loo argued that environmental justice 'requires coming to terms with the different scales' at which change is apprehended. The books — MacEachern on Atlantic parks (2001), Evenden on the Fraser (2004), Loo on wildlife (2006), Sandlos on northern game laws (2007), Piper on subarctic industry (2009), Parr on the senses (2010), Colpitts on pemmican (2014), Loo on relocation (2019) — won the CHA's prizes and, in Canadian PhD bibliographies, entered the company of Cronon, Worster and White in 2010–19 (MacEachern and Loo in 2010–14; Parr, Piper, Evenden and Sandlos in 2015–19; History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23). Loo (2014) asked the field to 'use more of the world, and vice versa'.
strands.works: NiCHE (2004); Nature | History | Society (UBC Press); Environmental History 12:4 (2007); MacEachern (2001), Evenden (2004), Loo (2006, 2019), Sandlos (2007), Piper (2009), Parr (2010), Colpitts (2014); Loo, 'Missed Connections' (2014)

strands.title: Conservation, dispossession and neighbouring historiographies
strands.focus: Cronon wrote that 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' showed 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995). Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks: Dispossessing the Wilderness traced how 'the early conception of the wilderness as the place where Indians lived (or should live)' gave way to 'the idealization of uninhabited wilderness' at Yellowstone, Glacier and Yosemite. Warren's The Hunter's Game (1997) and Jacoby's Crimes against Nature (2001; Marsh and Littleton-Griswold prizes), by Cronon's doctoral students, wrote the social history of poaching and conservation (unread; no reader read here links them to the wilderness essay). In Canada, Binnema and Niemi (2006) argued that the Stoney were excluded from Banff for game conservation, sport hunting, tourism and assimilation rather than for a wilderness ideal, and Sandlos (2007) that game laws and sanctuaries 'helped the state assert authority over traditional hunting cultures'; Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), with disease and climate among its causes, is blurbed by McNeill and read with Wolfe. The dissertation record records an associated readership pattern: the works newly co-cited with the field's founders after 2015 are Wolfe, Tuck and Yang, The Middle Ground, Hämäläinen, DuVal and O'Brien (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23; founders Cronon ×3, Worster ×3, White, Crosby, Merchant; lift ≥ 3; averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses). Settler colonial studies is its own entry; the link between the two is drawn there.
strands.works: Warren, The Hunter's Game (1997); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013)

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment; extended to 2024 on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) on the wilderness debate (Foreman 2000 read in full; the 1996 journal comments unread), the field's surveys (McNeill 2003 from the earlier record; Sutter 2013 by the editors' summary and abstract; Isenberg 2014 by abstract and contents), the Canadian field (NiCHE and UBC Press pages, publisher pages and abstracts 2001–2019) and the Anthropocene histories (publisher descriptions). The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 gives the readership: 5.7% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of the field's authors in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25 (Canada 10.2%, US 9.7%); the works co-cited with nine founding titles by Cronon, Worster, White, Crosby and Merchant (lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 and halved by 2020–25, the new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; the US network is stable in size, its entrants Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. The citation graph interprets these neighbourhoods as diffusion into neighbouring historiographies; this does not establish declining scholarly production or the field's own understanding of its development. The later texts named here are dated individually; the bodies of most are unread.

post.label: Postcolonial history / critique
post.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
post.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993). Lauren Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint), selected introduction on colonial difference and jurisdictional politics; contextual contribution, not a common postcolonial doctrine.

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988); A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000); edition with a new preface responding to critics (2007); “In Defense of Provincializing Europe” (2008)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality (1995); treats 'colonizer/colonized' as 'a historically shifting pair of social categories that needs to be explained' (2002, p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); asks scholars to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002). Gouda: homage to her work 'has become de rigueur' in postcolonial studies (2009).
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

representative_people.context: Metropole and colony in one frame: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, 1830–1867; read as postcolonial history by Woollacott (2006).
representative_people.works: Civilising Subjects (2002)

representative_people.context: Reads the French headscarf ban and the discourse of secularism as civilizational claims about gender equality, in the accounts of her reviewers Laborde and Whitney and her 2018 interview; Laborde finds the normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. Scott asks how to critique secularism without rejecting it (2018 interview).
representative_people.works: The Politics of the Veil (2007); Sex and Secularism (2017)

representative_people.context: Takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame that, in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them, reached India as an instrument of the East India Company, and asks historians to learn from literature the historicality of everyday life (2002), as Michael and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael fears the state may be lost “as an object of critique” and finds the argument largely conceptual.
representative_people.works: History at the Limit of World-History (2002)

representative_people.context: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography' and of 'history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'not all narratives or narrators are created equal'. Silencing the Past unread; wording awaits a library copy.
representative_people.works: Silencing the Past (1995)

representative_people.context: Investigates the making of colonial legal authority through cultural classifications, legal intermediaries and competing jurisdictions. Contextual legal history, not adherence to every postcolonial theory.
representative_people.works: “Colonial Law and Cultural Difference” (1999, body unread); Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint, introduction pp. 1–10 read)

representative_people.context: Uses the contact zone to analyze cultural encounter under asymmetrical power rather than presuming coherent, equal communities.
representative_people.works: “Arts of the Contact Zone” (1991); Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992; later second edition separate); Planetary Longings (2022 essay collection).

representative_people.context: Investigates colonial governing power through spatial and administrative arrangements.
representative_people.works: Colonising Egypt (1988; paperback preface 1991)

post.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Imperial knowledge and cultural authority
strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity
strands.focus: Colonial authority and identification are examined through unstable cultural meanings.

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality (1995). Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) made 'the intimate' a matter of state and 'colonizer/colonized' a shifting pair of categories (p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); the same year her 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' moved 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject', the programme now carried by the entry archival_turn.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper

strands.title: Cultural difference, legal forums and colonial authority
strands.focus: Benton treats legal classifications and forum disputes as elements in making colonial authority. The contests cut across divisions within colonizing and colonized populations. Her selected introduction asks how legal intermediaries and rival authorities altered the terms of rule; it does not treat either side as a coherent legal bloc or turn legal access into a guarantee of justice.
strands.works: Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint), chapter 1 pp. 1–10; “Colonial Law and Cultural Difference” (1999, abstract only).

strands.works: Imperial Meridian (1989); La colonisation de l’imaginaire (1988); Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: Competing narratives beyond national unity
strands.focus: Duara frames national, local and transnational histories as potentially conflicting rather than one evolutionary story.

strands.title: Comparison and connection in dispute
strands.focus: Lieberman’s state comparisons and Subrahmanyam’s circulation are interlocutory projects, not successive universal methods.

strands.title: Reciprocal comparison and connected units
strands.focus: Pomeranz names Wong’s reciprocal comparison and Tilly’s encompassing comparison as resources. Regions, states and wider systems answer different questions; the method does not require treating Europe and China as internally uniform.

strands.title: Proto-industry and the limits of trade
strands.focus: Pomeranz extends Mokyr’s labor model across regions while questioning unlimited manufacture exports and resource imports at unchanged relative prices. Comparing regions also requires examining their trading partners.

strands.title: Legal ordering across empires
strands.focus: Benton uses jurisdictional conflicts to ask how local cultural practices formed repeated institutional patterns across empires. This strategy places legal ordering alongside other ways of relating local encounters to global structures. Her 2002 introduction is read; the 2013 volume with Richard J. Ross and Stern’s separate 2011 corporate-sovereignty book are bibliographic resources, not evidence of a single school or transmission.
strands.works: Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint); Benton and Ross, eds., Legal Pluralism and Empires (2013, body unread). Further comparative resource: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011, publisher metadata only).

strands.title: Capitalism as connected regional diversity
strands.focus: In his 2020 methodological answer Beckert relates regional differences and connections: merchants, plantations, manufacturing and state power belong in the same global inquiry. His account resists treating Europe’s industrialisation as the whole history of capitalism. This strand records his stated strategy; the empirical adequacy of its global applications and criticism of the cotton argument remain open.
strands.works: GrowthPolicy interview with Devjani Roy (2020), answer 2; Empire of Cotton (2014, existing limited excerpt)

sts.label: Science and technology studies / STS
sts.description: An interdisciplinary field examining how knowledge, technologies, institutions, and social arrangements develop together. Historical, sociological, ethnographic, and policy-oriented inquiries coexist. SSK and laboratory studies contribute to STS but do not define its entire scope. Knorr Cetina’s comparative laboratory cultures, Harding’s feminist epistemology, and Sussex/Cornell institution building add distinct approaches and histories.
sts.representative_figures_and_works: Sheila Jasanoff, Gerald E. Markle, James C. Petersen, and Trevor Pinch, eds., Handbook of Science and Technology Studies (1995); Bruno Latour and Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life (1979). Hughes, Bijker and Pinch distinguish systems and constructionist technology research (1987); Jasanoff examines regulatory advice (1990); Haraway examines situated objectivity (1988).

philhistory.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
philhistory.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
philhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

philhistory.scope_note: Covering laws, understanding action, historical facts, and objectivity are different disputes; participants do not form a shared school. Hempel’s probabilistic sketches, Dray’s challenge, Carr’s reciprocal research and Mink’s comprehension are distinct. Primary readings and publisher-only contexts are explicitly separated.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.

historicalsociology.label: Comparative historical sociology
historicalsociology.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.
historicalsociology.representative_figures_and_works: Barrington Moore, Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966); Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979); Charles Tilly; Michael Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986); Perry Anderson (1974).

representative_people.context: Compares agrarian elites, peasants and political routes; violence accompanies even paths to democracy.
representative_people.works: Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966)

representative_people.context: Explains revolutionary breakdown and reconstruction through class relations, state organization and international pressures; later acknowledges shortcomings in her treatment of ideology.
representative_people.works: States and Social Revolutions (1979); “Cultural Idioms and Political Ideologies” (1985)

representative_people.context: Historical sociologist connecting political/economic transformations, collective struggles and repertoires; treats movements as historically specific.

representative_people.context: Distinguishes ideological, economic, military and political resources and their overlapping spatial networks.

representative_people.context: Treats historical social science as a challenge to fixed disciplinary boundaries and ahistorical universal laws. Williams’s framing (p. 203) and Wallerstein’s replies (pp. 206–207), read: historical systems, knowledge structures and disciplinary restructuring. The framing is attributed to Williams. A methodological contribution, without a founding claim or treating future-system predictions as established fact.
representative_people.works: Unthinking Social Science (1991); Open the Social Sciences (collective Gulbenkian Commission report, 1996)

historicalsociology.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Agrarian relations and political routes
strands.focus: Class alliances and rural power produce divergent, often violent paths rather than a smooth democratic sequence.

strands.title: States and revolutionary transformations
strands.focus: State organizations, agrarian classes and international competition enter a combined explanation.

strands.title: Contention and repertoires
strands.focus: Historically specific performances link local claims to wider transformations.
strands.works: Tilly, The Contentious French (1986); political-performances essay (1993–1994)

strands.title: Overlapping networks of power
strands.focus: Forms and reach of power are differentiated rather than enclosed in one homogeneous society.
strands.works: Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

strands.title: Comparative Marxian transitions
strands.focus: European transitions and divergent state forms frame a contested comparative synthesis.

strands.title: Authority, law and citizenship
strands.focus: Bendix compares authority; Somers examines how local relations and national law shape rights. Their methods are distinct.

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. This comparison retains structural-functional and evolutionary assumptions that his retrospective introduction discusses rather than simply disowns.
strands.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces

strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: State legibility and the limits of imposed plans
strands.focus: Scott asks how names, addresses, surveys and standards make societies open to administrative intervention, and how planning is altered by the social practices it encounters. His 2008 account also applies standardization to capitalist firms. These are comparative questions with attributed examples, not a single theory of every state.
strands.works: Seeing Like a State (1998); “Seeing Like a Society,” author interview (2008)

nationalismstudies.label: Nationalism studies
nationalismstudies.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.
nationalismstudies.representative_figures_and_works: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (1983); Hobsbawm and Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Anthony D. Smith; Partha Chatterjee, Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986).

representative_people.context: Connects national imagining to print markets and language; imagined communities are not thereby unreal.
representative_people.works: Imagined Communities (1983)

representative_people.context: Relates nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture; his reply to Smith allows varied cultural continuities.

nationalismstudies.scope_note: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm, Smith, and Chatterjee supply competing accounts, not a common modernist theory. Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

strands.title: Print markets and national imagining
strands.focus: Language and circulating print help make unfamiliar people imaginable as a community.

strands.title: Modern mobility and literate culture
strands.focus: The changing social role of culture supplies Gellner’s explanation; it is not merely a story of ancient identities awakening.

strands.title: Historically produced traditions
strands.focus: Rituals and claims of continuity have specific histories in national and imperial settings.

strands.title: Ethnic ties, myths and memories
strands.focus: Earlier cultural inheritances help explain particular nationalisms without making all nations timeless.
strands.works: The Ethnic Origins of Nations; Warwick opening

strands.title: Comparing national movements
strands.focus: Scholarship, agitation and mass participation are distinguished in a model attentive to social conditions and interrupted development.

strands.title: Anticolonial imagination and difference
strands.focus: The material/spiritual distinction identifies a claimed cultural domain of autonomy before political sovereignty.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993), pp. 4–7

strands.title: Routine reproduction of nationhood
strands.focus: Everyday language and symbols sustain belonging outside conspicuous nationalist movements.

strands.title: Gender, citizenship and national projects
strands.focus: Gender relations organize national reproduction and membership across, within and beyond state boundaries.

technology.label: History of technology
technology.description: Studies technological systems, invention, maintenance, use, and social change. Develops distinct institutions while exchanging questions with histories of science, economy, environment, and gender. Systems approaches and feminist studies of household technology show the range of its explanations. Wajcman’s feminist social-shaping questions and Bray’s Chinese domestic technologies broaden the field’s material and geographical examples.
technology.representative_figures_and_works: Society for the History of Technology (1958); Technology and Culture (1959); Thomas P. Hughes, Networks of Power (1983); Ruth Schwartz Cowan, More Work for Mother (1983). Pinch and Bijker (1984) investigate technological choices; their 1987 volume with Hughes makes the exchange with STS concrete.

representative_people.context: Compares electric power systems and their engineering, organizational and political settings.
representative_people.works: Networks of Power: Electrification in Western Society, 1880–1930 (1983)

representative_people.context: Shows how household technologies redistribute labour and interact with expectations of domestic work.
representative_people.works: More Work for Mother (1983)

consumption.label: Consumption & material culture
consumption.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.
consumption.representative_figures_and_works: McKendrick, Brewer, and Plumb, The Birth of a Consumer Society (1982); Appadurai, ed., The Social Life of Things (1986); Brewer and Porter, eds., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985). Additional readings: Douglas and Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979); Kopytoff on cultural biography (1986); de Vries on industrious change (1994); de Grazia and Furlough, The Sex of Things (1996). Maxine Berg and Helen Clifford, eds.: Consumers and Luxury (1999).

consumption.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Inventory evidence and its boundaries
strands.focus: Weatherill records selected goods across probate inventories. Missing laborers, debts, real estate and reliable clothing values constrain what household ownership can establish about society.

strands.title: Purchasing as household work
strands.focus: Vickery’s selected households distribute purchasing tasks and authority unevenly. Expenditure diaries show practical expertise, but incomplete income records limit reconstruction of financial power.

strands.title: Material meanings and unequal possibilities
strands.focus: Vickery finds social ambition alongside attachment and remembrance. Age, resources and inheritance matter; her chapter does not establish one feminine attitude to possessions.

strands.title: Competing chronologies and questions
strands.focus: Compare McKendrick’s eighteenth-century acceleration, Weatherill’s earlier middling ownership and de Vries’s household labor argument. Vickery questions universal motives. Different evidence and outcomes do not yield one automatic date for a consumer society.
strands.works: McKendrick (1982), introduction; Weatherill (1996), preface; de Vries (1994); Vickery (1998)

strands.title: Ming consumers and social distinctions
strands.focus: Clunas reads Wen Zhenheng’s judgments about appropriate objects as elite distinctions, then compares them with Yan Song’s confiscation inventory. These are different sources, not interchangeable records of actual purchasing.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.

strands.title: Luxury and European consumer culture
strands.focus: Berg and Clifford coedit a volume on luxury and consumer culture in Europe, 1650–1850. This records their editorial contribution; detailed chapter arguments remain unchecked.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

labourhistory.label: Labour history
labourhistory.date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s
labourhistory.description: Studies work, workers, labour relations and collective organisation across paid, unpaid, coerced, agricultural and industrial settings. Labour history includes unions and politics, workplace authority, household economies, culture, race, gender and colonial categories. Labour and labor are spelling variants; neither social history nor British Marxism exhausts the field.

labourhistory.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

romila_thapar.label: Romila Thapar
romila_thapar.date_label: Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961) · From Lineage to State (1984) · Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004) · The Past before Us (2013) · History as a Way of Remembering the Past (2014) · The Past as Present: Lahore keynote (2015)
romila_thapar.description: A historian of early India who joined textual and material evidence to questions of social change. The Library of Congress’s 2008 assessment emphasizes that methodological shift. In her 2014 methods chapter she distinguishes historical consciousness from conformity to modern European genres. Her 2015 Lahore lecture challenges inherited religious divisions of Indian history and reconstructs the changing uses of the Somanatha narrative. Talbot’s review presents The Past before Us as a study of the social purposes served by perceptions of the past. These are distinct inquiries, not a claim that every premodern narrative is reliable history.
romila_thapar.representative_figures_and_works: Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961); From Lineage to State (1984); Somanatha (2004); The Past before Us (2013); History as a Way of Remembering the Past (2014); The Past as Present (Lahore keynote, 2015).

gary_gerstle.label: Gary Gerstle
gary_gerstle.date_label: Working-Class Americanism (1989) · American Crucible (2001) · The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order (2022)
gary_gerstle.description: Historian of American labour,political economy and national belonging. Gerstle’s concept of a political order explains how a dominant movement can require opponents to accept its basic terms. His account of neoliberalism links bipartisan political settlement to capitalism’s globalization and later crises,while leaving the form of a successor order open. Earlier work connects labour and nationalism rather than assuming patriotic language is inherently conservative.

edmund_s_morgan.label: Edmund S Morgan
edmund_s_morgan.date_label: The Stamp Act Crisis (with Helen M.Morgan) (1953) · American Slavery,American Freedom (1975) · Inventing the People (1988)
edmund_s_morgan.description: Historian of early America who made the relation between slavery and freedom a central interpretive problem. In his1972 address,Morgan rejects treating enslavement as an exception to the national story or freedom as mere disguise. His Virginia-centered argument asks how racial domination and the independence claimed by white colonists developed together. Its particular mechanism remains open to debate rather than explaining every colonial society.

michel_vovelle.date_label: Piété baroque et déchristianisation en Provence (1973) · Idéologies et mentalités (1982) · La Mentalité révolutionnaire (article) (1991)
michel_vovelle.description: Historian of collective mentalities and the French Revolution who connected long changes in death and religion to moments of political rupture. In La Mentalité révolutionnaire,Vovelle asks whether slow transformations can accelerate in revolutionary crisis. His analysis treats hope and fear,violence and fraternity as interrelated,and explicitly rejects both unconditional devotion to the Revolution and blanket denunciation.

sidney_mintz.label: Sidney Mintz
sidney_mintz.date_label: Worker in the Cane1960 · Sweetness and Power1985 · Three Ancient Colonies2010
sidney_mintz.description: Sidney Mintz joined Caribbean fieldwork to histories of labour, slavery, markets and consumption. Worker in the Cane presents the narrated life of Eustaquio “Taso” Zayas; Sweetness and Power traces sugar through colonial production and changing diets. With Richard Price he investigated Afro-American cultural formation. Three Ancient Colonies compares Jamaica, Haiti and Puerto Rico. His anthropological training and fieldwork shaped historical inquiries that connect workers’ experiences, Caribbean societies and wider economic change.
sidney_mintz.representative_figures_and_works: Worker in the Cane: A Puerto Rican Life History (1960); Caribbean Transformations (1974); With Richard Price, An Anthropological Approach to the Afro-American Past: A Caribbean Perspective (1976); Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History (1985); Sweetness and Power — Penguin edition (1986); With Richard Price, The Birth of African-American Culture: An Anthropological Perspective — reissue with new preface (1992); Tasting Food, Tasting Freedom: Excursions into Eating, Culture, and the Past (1996); Three Ancient Colonies: Caribbean Themes and Variations (2010).
sidney_mintz.scope_note: Read Mintz’s three short author essays, selected2013 interview answers published2014, Leslie Rice’s1996 report, and Michiel Baud’s2011 review; complete monographs and the Mintz/Price primary essay and1992 preface remain unread. Baud’s reading of Caribbean Transformations is explicitly mediated, and he cautions that Three Ancient Colonies’s older fieldwork vignettes leave later migration, tourism and other changes insufficiently addressed.
